pages.x: For almost thirty years Ethiopia's government was dominated by the Tigray People's Liberation Front, the TPLF, from the northern region of Tigray. In 2018 a reformer, Abiy Ahmed, became prime minister, freed political prisoners and made peace with Eritrea. Sidelined, the TPLF's leaders withdrew to Tigray.

Abiy had won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019. In 2020 Tigray held its own election, defying the federal government, which had put off the national vote because of the pandemic. On 4 November Tigrayan forces attacked federal army bases in the region, and Abiy ordered an offensive, joined by Eritrean troops and forces from the Amhara region.

Federal troops took Mekelle, Tigray's capital, by the end of November, and Abiy said the operation was over. But the Tigrayan fighters melted into the mountains, and Tigray was cut off from the world, with its phones, internet and banks shut down.

Reports slowly leaked out of massacres, among them the killing of hundreds of civilians at Axum, by Eritrean soldiers according to rights groups, and of widespread rape. A joint inquiry by the UN and Ethiopia's rights commission found that all sides had committed abuses, some of which might be war crimes.
pages.of: civilians killed at Axum, rights groups said

pages.x: In June 2021 Tigrayan forces retook Mekelle, then pushed south into the Amhara and Afar regions, taking the holy town of Lalibela. By November they were less than 200 kilometres from Addis Ababa. Then, with newly bought armed drones, the army drove them back into Tigray.

For months little food or medicine reached Tigray's six million people, and the UN warned of famine. Aid groups and the UN said the government was blocking aid; the government blamed the Tigrayan forces.
pages.of: people in Tigray who needed food aid

pages.x: After a truce broke down, fighting began again in August 2022, and federal and Eritrean forces took Shire, Axum and Adwa. On 2 November 2022, in Pretoria, South Africa, the government and the TPLF signed a peace deal brokered by the African Union: Tigray's forces would disarm, and its services would be restored.

No one knows how many died. Researchers estimate that hundreds of thousands were killed by violence, hunger and the lack of medicine, which would make it one of the deadliest wars of the century so far. The peace largely held, but more than a million people were still unable to go home.
pts: Tigray was cut off from the world
Ended by the Pretoria deal in 2022
